newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban say they contain counter-attack.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban say they contain counter-attack.

text.p: Taleban officers said on Wednesday they had contained a major counter-attack in the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush mountains by forces of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, after fierce fighting.

"It was hard to contain the attacks and the fighting was very serious, but we brought up heavy reinforcements and halted it. We are now in control," said Maulavi Khairulla Haqani, the Salang battlefield commander of the purist Islamic Taleban militia which took Kabul on September 27.

But his front line at Qalatak, some 15 km (nine miles) north of the Taleban headquarter town of Jabal-os-Saraj was 15-20 km (nine to 13 miles) south of where it was before the attack began on Tuesday morning.

He refused to discuss casualties or where the reinforcements had come from at his front-line post, where the road was littered with shell casings and clearly exhausted and nervous Taleban fighters around him.
But western aid workers quoted witnesses in Jabal-os-Saraj as saying they had seen at least 100 dead Taleban and many more wounded being ferried from the battlefield.

"One counted 39 bodies being brought down in just one hour," one source said. They said the assault on the Taleban was led by Basir Solangi, Massod's commander in the Salang Pass who withdrew north into the territory of Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum as the Islamic militants pressed north from Kabul.

They said the attack had forced the Taleban to suspend their so-far unsuccessful attempt to break into Masood's Panjsher valley fortress from the town of Gulbahar astride the narrow, winding gorge leading into it.
"There are no Taleban left in Golbahar. They've all been switched to the Salang," said one.
He said the Taleban had suffered about 270 casualties since their attempt to force a way into the Panjsher began on Saturday, many of them to mines.

Golbahar lies about 10 km (six miles) east of Jabal-os-Saraj and the Panjsher valley runs northeast from there. The Salang Highway runs due north from Jabal-os-Saraj to Mazar-i-Sharif, from which Dostum controls six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces, and on to Central Asia.

The aid workers said Solangi moved down the pass and over the mountainsides to cut off a large Taleban force in an area of the winding, sheer-sided pass which included his own house, which a Taleban officer was using as his headquarters last week.

They said early on Wednesday Solangi, who destroyed a Soviet battalion in the area during the 1980s when Moscow backed a communist government in Kabul, controlled the mountain tops almost all the way to Jabal-os-Saraj.

However, at the Taleban front line later, black-turbanned warriors were scaling the mountainsides at Qalatak. It was not clear whether they had pushed Solangi back and Taleban fighters, speaking good English and saying they were from the Pakistani city of Karachi, expelled reporters who had reached there.
"Get out of here or we'll kill you," yelled one brandishing an automatic rifle. "Go straight to Kabul and don't stop on the way."

Taleban opponents have frequently accused Pakistan of backing the militia, a charge Islamabad denies. Reporters regularly meet Pakistani Taleban, but it is never clear whether they are Islamic militants or have connections to the Pakistani military.

Such anger is unusual on the front lines of the Taleban, who have swept to control, with few major setbacks, in three-quarters of Afghanistan since the movement was born in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago.
Usually, they are happy to chat about what is going on, but on Wednesday they were curt at best, suggesting that not all was going well for them.
Dostum appears to be moving towards an alliance with Masood, who has been his ally and his enemy in the past, and that would create the most serious opposition they have faced so far.
But Haqani said the Uzbeks who moved south down the the Salang Highway after the Taleban took Kabul, were not involved in the fighting on Tuesday and Wednesday morning.
He said, however, that two tanks did appear which might have belonged to Dostum, the former communist general with whom the Taleban say they would rather negotiate than fight.
